transcript.text:
The key first split is whether the freezer is still cold. If it is, the usual cause is restricted cold-air flow to the fridge: food blocking vents, an internal fan issue, or ice build-up from a defrost fault. If both sections are warm, settings, poor ventilation around the appliance, or a compressor/cooling fault become more likely. 1. Check the temperature setting is around 3–5°C for the fridge and -18°C for the freezer, with no holiday/eco mode selected. A wrong setting can cause this without a fault.
2. Check that food is not pressed against the internal vents or tightly packed around the back wall. Move anything blocking them; cold air has to circulate.
3. Look round both door seals for gaps, dirt or a folded section, and check the appliance has a little space around the back/sides. If safe to do so, switch it off and unplug it before gently vacuuming dust from any accessible rear or lower grille. Is the freezer still properly cold, and is there thick frost/ice on its rear wall?
[Helpful to see: image "Fridge not cooling — simple checks first" — Before suspecting the sealed system, check the temperature setting, that the door seal closes cleanly, that there's air space and clean condenser coils at the back, and listen for the compressor. Unplug before cleaning at the back. A sealed-system or refrigerant repair is a job for a qualified engineer. Typical layout — your model may differ.]
freezer still cold, about -17. yes thick frost on the back wall, more than ive ever seen. settings are 3 and -19, no one changed them

This points to a defrost-system ice blockage. With the freezer still around -17°C but an unusually thick sheet of frost on its rear wall, ice is likely stopping cold air reaching the fridge. The likely faulty area is the automatic defrost system — heater, defrost sensor/thermostat, or control/timer — rather than the temperature setting. 1. Switch the fridge-freezer off at the socket and unplug it. Move food to a cool box or another fridge/freezer, put towels down, and leave both doors open for 24–48 hours. It needs to be fully thawed, not just have the visible frost scraped off; do not use sharp tools or heat guns.
2. Dry it, switch it back on and allow roughly 12–24 hours with the doors mostly shut. If the fridge becomes cold again, that suggests the iced-up defrost area is the cause. If it cools after thawing but the frost returns over the following days or weeks, it needs an engineer to test the defrost heater, sensor/thermal cut-out and control. A manual defrost restores airflow temporarily but does not identify, or permanently cure, the failed component. If it does not cool again after a complete thaw, the freezer fan/airflow system becomes the next likely area to investigate.
ok will try the defrost. how long till I know if it worked? no burning smell or tripping btw

Once it has been fully thawed, allow about 12 hours for the fridge to start feeling properly cold again, and judge it after 24 hours with the doors kept mostly shut. The freezer can take up to 24 hours to settle back towards its normal temperature. So: a fridge back at roughly 3–5°C within 24 hours means the ice blockage was stopping the airflow. That suggests the fault area, but not the exact failed component. The longer-term test is whether the heavy frost returns: if it starts building up again over the next few days or weeks and the fridge warms again, the automatic defrost system is very likely at fault. An engineer would then test the defrost heater, sensor/thermal cut-out and control rather than replace parts blindly. If the fridge is still warm after a genuine 24–48 hour thaw and then 24 hours running, the next likely area is the freezer fan/air channel, and that is worth having checked.

candidates: Airflow/defrost ice build-up or internal fan problem (medium)
Temperature setting, blocked vents, door seal or poor ventilation around the appliance (medium)
